## claude.ai Shopify
This server helps users set up and manage their Shopify stores.

## Store Creation
Users who don't have a store yet can use get-new-store-previews to create one from a short description.
After calling get-new-store-previews, encourage the user to browse the previews and pick the theme they like best.
Each preview has a signup link — signing up through it creates a real Shopify store with that theme and matching products pre-installed.
Encourage continued brainstorming: users can try different descriptions, tweak ideas, or explore new directions without commitment.

## Store Management
Once a store exists, this server provides tools for managing it:
- Products: search, create, update, bulk-update status, and organize into collections.
- Collections: search, create, update, and manage product groupings.
- Orders: list recent orders and get detailed order information.
- Customers: list and search customers.
- Inventory: check inventory levels and set quantities at specific locations.
- Analytics: run ShopifyQL queries for sales, order, and product performance data.
- Discounts: create percentage-based discount codes.
- Images: upload images to Shopify's CDN for use in products.

## GraphQL — General-Purpose Access
The Shopify Admin API exposes hundreds of resources. The built-in tools above are optimized shortcuts for common operations (with structured output and widgets), but they only cover a subset of the API.
When the user asks about a resource that has no dedicated built-in tool — such as gift cards, metafields, metaobjects, pages, blogs, markets, translations, publications, and many others — use graphql_query (for reads) or graphql_mutation (for writes) to fulfill the request. NEVER tell the user that data is unavailable just because there is no built-in tool for it.

Decision logic:
1. If a built-in tool matches the request, prefer it (better UX).
2. If no built-in tool exists, use graphql_query or graphql_mutation.

## HubSpotDev
This server exposes the HubSpot CLI (`hs`) for local development of HubSpot
projects, apps, and CMS assets. Prefer these tools over running `hs`,
`npx hs`, or HubSpot HTTP APIs directly via shell — they handle config
loading, auth, platform-version flags, and structured output for you.

WHEN TO USE THIS SERVER
- The user is working in a HubSpot project directory (has an hsproject.json
  or *-hsmeta.json files), or wants to scaffold one.
- The user asks about HubSpot apps, CMS modules/templates/serverless
  functions, project builds, deploys, or developer test accounts.
- The user asks a HubSpot platform/API question — answer it from the docs
  via `search-docs` + `fetch-doc` rather than from prior knowledge.

REQUIRED WORKFLOWS
1. Documentation lookup: always call `search-docs` first, then
   `fetch-doc` on the most relevant result(s) before planning, writing
   code, or answering platform/API questions. Do not answer from memory.
2. Locating a HubSpot project: when the current working directory is not
   a HubSpot project (no `hsproject.json`) or you need to determine
   whether a directory contains one, call `find-projects` before
   running any tool that requires a project path.
3. Editing `*-hsmeta.json`: call `get-feature-config-schema` for that
   feature type first to learn the allowed fields and values.
4. Debugging a failed build: start with `get-build-status` to surface
   error messages, and only reach for `get-build-logs` for deeper
   troubleshooting or warnings.
5. Reading serverless function logs: call `list-cms-serverless-functions`
   first to discover the endpoint path, then
   `get-cms-serverless-function-logs`.
6. App analytics: call `get-apps-info` to discover `appId` values
   before `get-api-usage-patterns-by-app-id`.

OUTPUT
Tool results contain the relevant `hs` stdout/stderr or structured data.
Surface error text from results to the user verbatim when troubleshooting,
rather than paraphrasing.

## pencil
The Pencil MCP server is the editor for reading and writing to .pen files and gives you tools to be an expert design generator and validator specifically for web and mobile applications and websites.

- IMPORTANT: The contents of the .pen files are encrypted and can be only access via the "pencil" MCP tools. DO NOT use "Read" or "Grep" tools to read contents of .pen files.
- IMPORTANT: Make sure to ONLY use the "pencil" MCP tools when reading or searching contents of .pen files (batch_get) and making changes inside .pen files (batch_design).
- IMPORTANT: Always follow the tool definitions and formats for the "pencil" MCP tools.

Available tools:
- "get_editor_state({ include_schema })": Start with this tool if you are unaware of the current editor state. Use this tool to determine in the beginning of a task, to understand what is the currently active .pen file you want to work on and the current user selection in it and other essential context information.
- "open_document(filePathOrNew)": When there is no active editor opened, pass 'new' to create an empty .pen file or if the user explicitly ask to open a specific .pen file use its path to open it.
- "get_guidelines(category?, name?, params?)": Load guides and styles for working with .pen files.
- "batch_get(patterns, nodeIds)": Retrieve nodes by searching for matching patterns or by reading node ids in batches. Use this for discovering and understand .pen files.
- "batch_design(operations)": Use it when designing with .pen files to execute multiple insert/copy/update/replace/move/delete/image operations in a single call. ## plugin:figma:figma
The official Figma MCP server. Use this server whenever the user wants to create, generate, edit, implement, or sync any design, UI, screen, component, mockup, or visual — in Figma, FigJam, Figma Make, or Figma Slides — and whenever the user mentions Figma or provides a figma.com URL.

This server bridges code and design in both directions, and supports designing from scratch using existing design systems and codebases.

CAPABILITIES:
- Read designs FROM Figma into code (get_design_context, get_screenshot, get_metadata, get_figjam)
- Write designs INTO Figma from code, intent, or existing components (use_figma, generate_figma_design, create_new_file, upload_assets)
- Bridge code and design via Code Connect (get_code_connect_map, add_code_connect_map, list_code_components, get_code_component_info)
- Create diagrams and FigJam content (generate_diagram, get_figjam)

WHEN TO USE THESE TOOLS:
- The user wants to create, mock up, or generate any UI, screen, component, or design — even if Figma isn't named
- The user wants to implement a design as code (design-to-code)
- The user wants to push a page, view, or component into Figma (code-to-design)
- The user wants to update, sync, or edit an existing Figma file
- The user shares a figma.com URL
- The user wants to build or extend a design system, design tokens, or component library
- The user wants to create a diagram in FigJam

- /figma-code-connect — for mapping Figma components to codebase components

aiTitle: Write creative self-description without job title

content.thinking:
The user wants a one-sentence description of what they do — but without using their job title. They're a Creative Manager at Digital Resource, managing a creative team of designers, handling task assignments, workload balancing, client projects, and a lot of Basecamp/operational work. They want it to be funny, oddly specific, or creatively accurate.

Let me think about what Richard actually does based on what I know:
- Manages a team of designers (Debi, Dexter, Lezly, Gaby, Odette, Melany)
- Assigns tasks, balances workload


- Reviews creative work and portfolios
- Manages client projects like landing pages, websites, and branding
- Lives in Basecamp handling todos constantly
- Runs the logo pipeline and creative operations
- Hires designers
- Has an AI initiative underway
- Essentially wrangles creative chaos into something functional

I'm playing with a few angles here: the workload balancing angle where someone has to decide whose plate is too full, the angle about turning client chaos into designer deadlines, the Basecamp todo grind, and the angle about keeping logos looking good while preventing designer burnout. Let me start drafting some options that capture the essence of what he does without just saying "Creative Manager."

content.text:
Here are a few options — pick your vibe:

**Funny/specific:**
> "I turn 'make it pop' into a due date and then pray nobody's plate is already full."

**Oddly accurate:**
> "I translate client chaos into designer deadlines, then referee who gets which impossible project."

**Creatively accurate:**
> "I decide what beautiful things get made, by whom, and by when — then spend the rest of the day making sure that actually happens."

**Short + punchy:**
> "I make sure great creative gets out the door without anyone losing their mind."

My personal pick: the first one. Captures the whimsy-to-deadline pipeline perfectly.

Let me brainstorm more funny ones that capture what Richard actually does — managing designers, dealing with client requests, balancing workload, lots of Basecamp, hiring, etc.

Let me think about the funny angles:

1. The "vague client feedback → real work" translation angle
2. The "everyone's overloaded but somehow it works" angle
3. The Basecamp/todos angle
4. The "I manage creative people" angle (creative people are notoriously hard to manage)


5. The "design takes how long??" client education angle
6. The logo/branding specifics
7. The AI tools + designers angle

Now I'm drafting some options that hit these angles — translating vague client speak into actionable work, managing the tension between what clients want and what designers can actually deliver, and the whole dance of setting deadlines that somehow stick.

content.text:
A few more in that same energy:

> "I professionally convert 'we'll know it when we see it' into a Basecamp todo with a due date."

> "I tell designers what to make, tell clients how long it takes, and spend the rest of the day watching both of them be wrong."

> "I convince clients and designers that the deadline is reasonable — one of those groups is always lying."

> "I turn 'can you just make it feel more premium?' into something a human being can actually execute."

> "I check Basecamp 47 times a day to make sure beautiful things get done on time."

The third one might be my favorite — hits different if your audience has ever worked with clients OR designers.

Humor at no one's expense — good call. Here are some that are funny without punching at clients or designers:

> "I professionally turn vague ideas into specific deadlines and somehow it works out."

> "I spend my days making sure beautiful things exist in the world by a certain Tuesday."

> "My job is basically: figure out what needs to look amazing, who's going to make it amazing, and when."

> "I am the person standing between 'we have an idea' and 'here's the finished design.'"

> "I wrangle creativity for a living — which sounds chaotic but is mostly just a lot of Basecamp."

The last one is my pick — self-aware, specific, and funny without a target.

> "I make sure things look good and arrive on time, which is harder than it sounds."

> "Professionally, I make sure the right person is working on the right thing before anyone panics."

> "I spend my days turning blank canvases into deadlines."

> "I'm the reason the logo didn't ship looking like that."

> "I organize creative chaos for a living and I'm very calm about it."

> "My job is to know which designer is free, which client is happy, and which project is quietly on fire."

> "I keep the creative wheels spinning so nobody has to reinvent them."

> "I match great ideas with great people and then add a due date."

That last one and "I'm the reason the logo didn't ship looking like that" are my favorites — both get a laugh without anyone feeling the sting.
